hints: Start by thinking about the main job of blood plasma - what kinds of substances must it pick up, carry and deliver around the body?
Recall the structure of a water molecule - it is dipolar with slightly positive hydrogen and slightly negative oxygen. How does this help it interact with ions and polar molecules?
Think about heat - blood must not change temperature quickly as it moves. Which thermal property of water resists rapid temperature change?
walkthrough:
Why blood needs a solvent**
Blood plasma carries many dissolved substances between organs, such as nutrients, salts, urea for excretion and hormones. A good transport medium must be able to dissolve them and keep them in solution.

Polarity makes water a good solvent**
Water molecules are dipolar, so the slightly positive and slightly negative regions attract charged ions and other polar molecules. This surrounds solutes and keeps them dissolved, allowing blood to transport them easily.

High specific heat capacity stabilises temperature**
Water needs a lot of heat energy to raise its temperature by $1 ^{\circ}\text{C}$. This high specific heat capacity means blood resists sudden warming or cooling, so heat picked up from the liver and muscles is spread evenly and body temperature stays fairly constant.

Final answer: Water is a good solvent for ions and polar molecules, so plasma transports dissolved substances e.g. glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones; water has a high specific heat capacity, so blood temperature remains fairly constant and heat is distributed around the body.

hints: Follow the arrows on Fig. 2.1 - vessel P leaves the left side of the heart and flows down to the body tissues, while vessel Q returns blood up to the right side of the heart. Which large artery and large vein do these jobs?
walkthrough:
Trace the flow**
On the right side of the diagram, vessel P carries blood away from the left ventricle downwards to the capillary bed of the body organs. That is the main systemic artery. On the left side, vessel Q carries blood upwards from the body organs back into the right atrium. That is the main systemic vein.

Name the vessels**
The artery leaving the left ventricle to the body is the aorta. The vein returning blood from the body to the right atrium is the vena cava.
Final answer: P - aorta; Q - vena cava.

hints: Compare what type of blood each vessel carries - think about where the blood has just come from, the lungs or the respiring tissues?
Now think about destination and pressure - where is P sending blood to, and where is Q sending blood to, and which one has just left the pumping ventricle?
walkthrough:
Function of P**
P is the aorta. It has just received oxygenated blood from the left ventricle, the strongest pump. It delivers this oxygenated blood at high pressure out to the organs and respiring tissues of the systemic circulation.

Function of Q**
Q is the vena cava. It collects deoxygenated blood from the veins of the body after oxygen has been released to tissues, and returns it at low pressure to the right atrium of the heart to be sent to the lungs.

Final answer: P / aorta transports oxygenated blood at high pressure to the body organs / respiring tissues / systemic circulation; Q / vena cava transports / returns deoxygenated blood at low pressure to the right atrium / heart.

hints: Think about the word closed - does blood ever leave vessels to bathe tissues directly, or does it stay inside heart, arteries, capillaries and veins?
Count how many times blood goes through the heart on one full trip around the body - trace from heart to lungs to heart to body to heart.
walkthrough:
Why closed**
In a mammal, blood never leaves the system of tubes. It stays inside the heart, arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules and veins all the way round. Substances leave by diffusion or filtration, but the blood cells and most plasma stay contained. That is a closed circulation.

Why double**
Follow one red cell: heart to lungs, back to heart, then out to body, back to heart. It goes through the heart twice per complete circuit. The heart to lungs and back loop is the pulmonary circulation, and the heart to body and back loop is the systemic circulation.

Final answer: Closed - blood is contained within vessels / heart, arteries, capillaries and veins throughout; double - blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit, once in pulmonary circulation and once in systemic circulation.

hints: Look ahead to where blood goes next - thin-walled capillaries. What would happen if blood at $12.7 \text{kPa}$ hit those delicate walls directly?
Think about the job of capillaries - exchange by diffusion needs time and a very thin barrier. How does lower pressure and slower flow help?
walkthrough:
Protecting delicate capillaries**
Capillary walls are only one thin layer of endothelial cells to allow rapid diffusion. They cannot withstand high pressure and would burst or be damaged if arterial pressure reached them unchanged. Arterioles act as a pressure drop zone.

Allowing effective exchange**
Lower pressure means slower flow through the capillary network. Slow movement gives more time for oxygen, glucose, amino acids and other materials to diffuse out, and for carbon dioxide and wastes to diffuse in, making exchange efficient.

Final answer: High pressure would burst / damage thin-walled capillaries, which are one endothelial cell thick; at low pressure blood flows slowly allowing time for exchange / diffusion of substances.

hints: Start with what they share - recall the three basic layers of all arteries. Which linings are present in both a muscular artery and an arteriole?
Now compare size - think about lumen width and the ratio of wall thickness to lumen in the small arteriole in Fig. 2.2 versus a larger muscular artery.
Think about how wall composition changes with size - which vessel needs more smooth muscle, elastic fibres and collagen to withstand and control higher pressure?
walkthrough:
Similarities - the basic plan**
Both vessels are built to the same plan. Inside is a smooth endothelium, the tunica intima, which reduces friction. Outside that both have a tunica media containing smooth muscle to control diameter.

Difference in proportions**
A muscular artery is larger overall. It has a wider lumen than the arteriole in Fig. 2.2, but its wall is much thicker relative to that lumen. In the arteriole the wall is thin compared with the lumen, giving a smaller wall to lumen ratio.

Difference in wall tissues**
Because the muscular artery carries blood at higher pressure ($12.7 \text{kPa}$) and helps distribute it, it has a much thicker layer of smooth muscle, more elastic fibres to stretch and recoil, and more collagen to resist tearing. The arteriole has only a thin layer of smooth muscle and little or no elastic lamina, which is enough for vasoconstriction to control flow into capillaries.

Final answer: Similarities: both have endothelium / tunica intima; both have tunica media / smooth muscle. Differences: muscular artery has thicker wall / smaller lumen to wall thickness ratio; wider lumen; more / thicker layer of smooth muscle; more elastic fibres / tissue; more collagen fibres than arteriole.
